headings.title: Introduction to Standard Precautions in Nursing
headings.content:
Standard precautions are the foundational baseline infection prevention practices applied to the care of all patients in healthcare settings, regardless of their diagnosed or presumed infection status. Developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, these measures recognize that any patient can harbor bloodborne or other infectious pathogens. In busy clinical units across Nigeria, from bustling federal teaching centres to rural primary healthcare clinics, assuming that infection risk is only present in isolated rooms leaves healthcare personnel vulnerable. 

The core principle is simple yet vital: treat all blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes as potentially infectious. By embedding these habits into routine nursing procedures—such as bed bath administration, wound dressing, and perineal care—practitioners create an invisible shield protecting both themselves and the vulnerable populations they serve.

headings.title: The Chain of Infection and Rationale for Precautions
headings.content:
Infection transmission relies on a continuous chain of six links: the infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. If any single link is broken, the chain collapses and infection is prevented. Standard precautions primarily target the mode of transmission and portals of entry or exit.

Pathogens travel via contact, droplets, or airborne routes. Understanding this microbial journey transforms routine tasks from mechanical chores into deliberate biological defenses. For instance, wearing a barrier prevents direct skin contact with an infectious reservoir, effectively stopping transmission before a susceptible host can be colonized.

headings.title: Hand Hygiene Practices and Techniques
headings.content:
Hand hygiene is universally acknowledged as the single most critical intervention for preventing healthcare-associated infections. Microorganisms on human hands are categorized into transient flora, picked up through direct patient contact and easily removed, and resident flora, which inhabit deeper skin layers. 

- **Alcohol-based hand rub**: Preferred when hands are not visibly soiled; requires vigorous friction until dry, covering all surfaces.
- **Plain or antimicrobial soap and water**: Indicated when hands are visibly dirty, soiled with proteinaceous material, or after caring for patients with spore-forming pathogens like Clostridioides difficile.

Timing matters immensely. Nurses must perform hand hygiene before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings.

headings.title: Selection and Proper Use of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
headings.content:
Personal protective equipment acts as a physical barrier between the healthcare worker and infectious materials. Selecting the correct item depends on the anticipated nature of the clinical interaction and potential exposure route.

| PPE Item | Primary Clinical Indication |
| --- | --- |
| Gloves | Anticipated contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, or non-intact skin |
| Gown | Preventing soiling of clothing during procedures likely to generate splashes |
| Mask and Eye Protection | Protecting mucous membranes of eyes, nose, and mouth during procedures generating sprays |
| Respirator (N95) | Preventing inhalation of small airborne droplet nuclei |

The sequence of putting on (donn) and taking off (doff) PPE is non-negotiable. Donning typically follows gown, mask, goggles, then gloves. Doffing requires careful removal to avoid self-contamination, usually starting with gloves, followed by goggles, gown, and finally the mask, paired with immediate hand hygiene.

headings.title: Safe Injection Practices and Sharps Management
headings.content:
Sharps injuries pose a severe occupational hazard for nursing staff, risking transmission of bloodborne viruses such as Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV. Safe injection practices protect both patients and providers.

- **Never recap needles**: Using two hands to recap a used needle is a leading cause of accidental sharps puncture.
- **Use safety devices**: Whenever available, activate engineered sharps injury protection mechanisms immediately after use.
- **Immediate disposal**: Drop used needles, syringes, and lancets directly into a puncture-resistant, leak-proof sharps container located at the point of use.
- **Do not overfill**: Seal and replace sharps containers once they reach the designated fill line, typically three-quarters full.

headings.title: Respiratory Hygiene and Cough Etiquette
headings.content:
Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette were institutionalized globally to curtail the spread of respiratory pathogens dispersed through droplets and secretions. Patients, visitors, and staff must be educated and supported to practice these habits from the moment they enter a healthcare facility.

Key elements include covering the mouth and nose with a tissue when coughing or sneezing, disposing of used tissues promptly into the nearest waste receptacle, and performing hand hygiene immediately afterward. When tissues are unavailable, coughing or sneezing into the inner elbow rather than bare hands prevents the transfer of pathogens to environmental surfaces and door handles. Healthcare facilities should provide accessible hand sanitizer stations and tissue boxes at triage and waiting areas.

headings.title: Environmental Cleaning and Patient Care Equipment Handling
headings.content:
The hospital environment acts as a reservoir for resilient pathogens capable of surviving on dry surfaces for weeks or months. Standard precautions dictate that reusable patient care equipment—such as blood pressure cuffs, glucometers, thermometers, and stethoscopes—must be meticulously cleaned and disinfected between patients.

Routine cleaning removes organic soil, while disinfection inactivates specific microorganisms. High-touch surfaces, including bed rails, bedside tables, light switches, and door knobs, require frequent cleaning with hospital-approved disinfectants. Nurses must verify that equipment manufacturers' guidelines are followed regarding contact times and chemical compatibility to ensure effective microbial destruction without damaging delicate devices.

headings.title: Management of Healthcare-Associated Exposures and Spills
headings.content:
Despite rigorous adherence to safety protocols, accidents occur. When blood or body fluid spills happen, or when a healthcare worker sustains an occupational exposure via needle stick, mucous membrane splash, or broken skin, immediate action is mandatory.

For percutaneous or skin exposures, the site must be washed immediately with soap and running water; antiseptic washes or harsh scrubbing are discouraged as they can damage tissue and enhance pathogen entry. Splashes to the eyes or mucous membranes require prompt flushing with copious amounts of clean water or normal saline. Following first aid, the incident must be reported immediately to the designated occupational health officer or ward supervisor to initiate prompt risk assessment, documentation, and potential post-exposure prophylaxis for bloodborne viruses.
